title: Private Label Sunscreen Manufacturer in India: Filters, SPF Testing, Rules and Process

description: Choosing a private label sunscreen manufacturer in India? Compare filter routes, SPF and PA tests, BIS and label rules, the 8-stage process and key questions.
image_alt: Model applying sunscreen made by a private label sunscreen manufacturer in India
body_html:
Sunscreen is the product Indian shoppers now question hardest: they read the SPF number, look for PA plus signs, test the white cast in the store and check whether the claim was proven on skin. For a brand founder, that makes the choice of private label sunscreen manufacturer more important than for almost any other launch. A good partner hands you a formula that is already tested, a filter system that suits Indian skin tones, and the paperwork to stand behind every number printed on the tube.

This guide covers the choices to make before you approach a factory, how SPF testing in India works, the rules that touch a sun care label, the stages of third party sunscreen manufacturing and the questions worth asking. We make sunscreens for brands at our Ambala plant, so we also explain how we run these projects. Sources are listed at the end.

What a private label sunscreen manufacturer does (and what stays with you)

In private label sun care, the manufacturer brings a developed, tested base and you bring the brand, adjusting fragrance, texture, tint, pack and SPF level. A brand-new filter system or claim moves the project into custom formulation, with longer timelines and fresh testing. Our article on private label, contract manufacturing and custom formulation sets out that choice in detail.

A typical split of work looks like this:

  • Manufacturer: base formula, filter selection within legal limits, lab samples, stability checks in your chosen pack, arranging SPF and PA testing, batch production, quality release, filling and dispatch, all under its own manufacturing licence.
  • Your brand: positioning, price, pack design, label approval, marketing and distribution.
  • Shared: the claim list, which must stay inside what the test reports support.

Mineral vs chemical sunscreen: pick the filter system first

Feel, finish, white cast, photostability and the claim story all follow from the UV filters. Founders often start with "SPF 50, matte, no white cast"; the formulator translates that into one of four filter routes.

Filter routeWhat protects the skinStrengthsTrade-offs to plan for
MineralZinc oxide (with or without titanium dioxide)Gentle positioning, broad UVA and UVB cover from one filter, a strong story for sensitive skin and kidsNeeds careful dispersion to avoid a grey or white film on medium and deep skin tones
Chemical (new-generation)Organic filters such as Tinosorb S, Tinosorb M and Uvinul T 150Clear, light textures; easy to make fluid or gel formatsFilter levels must stay within permitted limits; photostability must be shown
HybridOrganic filters plus zinc oxideHigh protection with a softer cast than pure mineralMore complex label and ingredient story
TintedMineral or hybrid base with iron oxide pigmentsHides residual cast, adds visible-light benefit claims only if testedShade range must suit Indian skin tones; more SKUs to stock

Our own sun care work covers all four routes, plus bi-phasic SPF serums, cooling fluids and mineral body sprays. For a deeper look at how zinc oxide is dispersed so it spreads clear, see our post on mineral sunscreen without white cast.

Match the route to your buyer: oily-skin city buyers tend to want a matte fluid or gel, sensitive-skin and baby ranges lean mineral and fragrance-free, and outdoor buyers want sweat resistance, which needs its own test.

SPF and PA testing: what a private label sunscreen needs

An SPF number on a pack is a measured result, not a recipe target, and two kinds of test exist.

In vitro tests are run in a lab on a roughened plate. They are quick and cheap, so formulators use them to compare prototypes. In vivo tests are run on human volunteers. Under ISO 24444, small areas of skin on each volunteer are exposed to graded doses from a solar simulator, with and without the product, and a trained evaluator reads the redness 16 to 24 hours later. The ANSI summary of the standard notes that "a minimum of 10 volunteers are typically used". UVA protection, shown in India as PA+ to PA++++, is measured by its own methods: ISO 24442 on volunteers, or ISO 24443 in the lab.

India has adopted these international methods as Indian Standards. The BIS catalogue lists IS 17493:2021 as identical to ISO 24443 for in vitro UVA protection, and IS 17494:2021 as the Indian version of ISO 24444 for in vivo SPF (the catalogue currently shows IS 17494 as withdrawn, and says standards published after October 2025 sit on its new portal). In 2026 BIS also issued a product standard for sunscreens; the regulatory publisher ChemLinked reports it as "IS 19685: 2026 Sunscreen Cosmetics Products - Specification". Ask your manufacturer how its test plan lines up with the current version before you print a claim.

Why a higher tested SPF is worth having

SPF tests apply the product at 2 mg per square centimetre. Real users put on much less. A study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology measured labelled SPF 70 and SPF 100 products at a quarter of the test dose and reported actual values of 19 and 27; the authors noted that consumers typically apply "from 0.5 to 1 mg/cm(2)". The chart below shows that gap. It is one reason many Indian brands now launch at SPF 50 and above, and why clear usage directions on the pack matter.

Indian rules that touch a sunscreen launch

In India a sunscreen sold for skin protection is regulated as a cosmetic under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, administered by CDSCO and the state licensing authorities. In practice, a private label sunscreen launch has to get these points right:

  1. Manufacturing licence. The product must be made at a site holding a valid cosmetic manufacturing licence. If your brand uses the manufacturer's licence through a loan licence route, read our guide to the cosmetic loan licence.
  2. Permitted filters and limits. Each UV filter has an allowed maximum level. Ask the factory to show you the reference it used for every filter in your formula.
  3. Label content. The Cosmetics Rules list what labels must carry (name, manufacturer and address, licence and batch numbers, dates, ingredients, warnings); the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules add net quantity, MRP and consumer care details.
  4. Claims. Every SPF, PA, water resistance, "broad spectrum" or "non-comedogenic" statement needs a report behind it. Avoid drug-style wording such as "treats" or "prevents disease"; a cosmetic sunscreen protects against sunburn and helps reduce UV damage.
  5. BIS standards. Check the current BIS sunscreen standards with your manufacturer, as the catalogue has changed during 2025 and 2026.

The private label sunscreen process, step by step

Most of a sunscreen project is spent proving the product, not making it.

  • Brief: give the filter route, SPF and PA target, finish, pack size, retail price and one benchmark. Our product brief form asks for exactly these.
  • Wear trial: try samples on several skin tones, on bare skin and under makeup; note pilling, eye sting and how the cast looks after ten minutes.
  • Lock, then test: any change to filters, emollients or pigment can shift the SPF result, so freeze the formula before testing and keep the reports in the batch file.
  • Stability in the final pack: zinc oxide can settle and emulsions can split in heat; testing in the real tube or pump catches this early.

One base, several SPF levels: planning a sunscreen range

A new sunscreen brand in India rarely needs many formulas at launch. A practical set is a daily face PA++++ sunscreen at SPF 50, a tinted variant of the same base, and later a higher SPF or a body spray for summer. Keeping one base across the range keeps the feel consistent, simplifies stability work and lets you reorder in combined batches. Our mineral base, for example, uses 25% zinc oxide with no titanium dioxide and scales from SPF 15 to SPF 70 with the same texture; each level still needs its own test report before it is labelled.

Packaging choices for private label sunscreen

Tubes are the usual choice: light, low cost and protective against air. Airless pumps suit fluids and give a measured dose; sprays need a matched valve and a sprayable formula; sticks need a different base altogether. Include the chosen pack in stability testing and leave enough label space for the mandatory declarations and directions.

Questions to ask a private label sunscreen manufacturer

A capable sunscreen maker answers these quickly and in writing.

  1. Which filter routes do you already have tested bases for, and in which formats?
  2. Are the SPF and PA results for this base from in vivo tests on the final formula, and can I see the reports?
  3. How does your test plan line up with the current BIS sunscreen standards?
  4. What can I change (tint, fragrance, texture) without needing a new SPF test?
  5. What stability data do you have in the pack I plan to use, and at what storage conditions?
  6. What is the minimum batch in kilograms, and how many filled units does it give in my pack size?
  7. Do you hold a valid cosmetic manufacturing licence for this product category, and who files the product details?
  8. What is the typical time from approved sample to dispatched first batch?

Our checklist for choosing a third-party cosmetic manufacturer covers the broader factory checks, such as audits and quality systems.

faqs.q: How do I start a private label sunscreen brand in India?
faqs.a: Decide who you are selling to and which filter route suits them (mineral, chemical, hybrid or tinted). Brief a licensed manufacturer with your target SPF and PA, texture, pack and price, approve samples, lock the formula, test stability in your pack, get in vivo SPF and PA reports, and print only the claims those reports support.

faqs.q: Is SPF testing mandatory for sunscreen in India?
faqs.a: Any SPF or PA value printed on a pack must be backed by test data, and BIS has published sunscreen test methods and, in 2026, a sunscreen product standard. In vivo testing on volunteers is the accepted basis for label claims. Confirm the current BIS requirements with your manufacturer before launch.

faqs.q: What is the difference between in vitro and in vivo SPF?
faqs.a: In vitro SPF is measured in a laboratory on a plate and is used to screen and compare prototypes. In vivo SPF is measured on human volunteers using a method such as ISO 24444 and is what label claims should rest on.

faqs.q: Which is better for a new brand, mineral or chemical sunscreen?
faqs.a: Neither is better for every buyer. Mineral suits sensitive-skin, baby and gentle positioning but needs good dispersion to avoid white cast. New-generation chemical filters give clear, light textures. Hybrids sit in between. Choose the route your target customer will wear every day.

faqs.q: What does PA++++ mean on a sunscreen?
faqs.a: PA shows the level of UVA protection, graded from PA+ to PA++++, with PA++++ the highest grade. It is based on a UVA test such as ISO 24442 on volunteers, so it needs its own report alongside the SPF result.

faqs.q: Can I launch several SPF levels from one formula?
faqs.a: Often yes. A well-designed base can be adjusted to different SPF levels while keeping the same feel, which keeps a range consistent. Each SPF level is a separate product for testing and labelling, so each needs its own report.

faqs.q: How long does it take to make a private label sunscreen?
faqs.a: Sampling is the quick part; at Ecosmetix lab samples are typically ready in about 14 days. Stability checks in the final pack, SPF and PA testing, artwork and production add to the total, so plan the launch around testing time.

faqs.q: Can a sunscreen claim to be water resistant?
faqs.a: Only if it has passed a water resistance test on volunteers. That test is separate from the standard SPF test, so ask your manufacturer to include it in the plan if you want the claim.
